questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: The sexual cycle as an ordering
questions.learningObjective: Write the sexual life cycle of a mushroom in the correct order.
questions.stem: The survey card asks the cartographer to write out the sexual life cycle of a mushroom in order.

answer.exemplar: Two compatible haploid mycelia of opposite mating types meet and their hyphae fuse, so the cytoplasms join while the two haploid nuclei remain separate. This produces a dikaryotic mycelium, in which each cell holds two haploid nuclei and a clamp connection keeps them in neighbouring compartments. In the basidium the two nuclei fuse, giving one diploid nucleus, and meiosis then produces four haploid nuclei. Each of these moves out along a sterigma into a basidiospore, which is released and germinates to restart the haploid cycle.

questions.explanation: The order matters: cytoplasmic fusion first, a period with two separate haploid nuclei second, then nuclear fusion and meiosis. Any sequence that puts meiosis before karyogamy breaks the cycle.
questions.hint: Fuse cytoplasm, then fuse nuclei, then halve.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Plan a test for arbuscular mycorrhizal colonisation of plant roots.
questions.stem: The projection plan for survey work asks how a team could test whether plant roots are colonised by arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.

answer.exemplar: Collect fine root tips from the plant and the nearby soil, clear them in a mild alkali, stain them with a fungal stain such as acid fuchsin or trypan blue, and mount them for microscopy. Score each root segment for the presence of arbuscules, vesicles and intraradical hyphae, and compare the percentage colonised with roots from a plant grown without fungal inoculum. Recover the fungal DNA from the same roots and sequence it to confirm that the partner belongs to a glomeromycete lineage.

questions.explanation: Microscopy shows the characteristic arbuscules and vesicles inside the root cortex, and DNA sequencing confirms which fungal partner is present. Uncolonised control roots rule out staining artefacts.
questions.hint: Stain cleared root tips and look for arbuscules.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a hymenium produces such large numbers of spores.
questions.stem: The projection manual asks for an explanation of why a hymenium produces so many spores.

answer.exemplar: A hymenium packs thousands of basidia into a small area, and each basidium releases four spores from sterigmata, so the tissue produces spores in very large numbers. That output raises the chance that a spore lands on a substrate where it can germinate. The dense arrangement also lets the spores be shed together in a puff, which carries them clear of the cap and away from the parent mycelium.

questions.explanation: The explanation rests on the density of basidia in the layer, the four spores each one makes, and the shared puff that disperses them. The dispersal benefit should stay tied to the numbers produced.
questions.hint: Connect the density of basidia with spore dispersal.

questions.learningObjective: Design a test showing that a white rot fungus degrades lignin.
questions.stem: The projection plan for timber plots asks how a survey team could show that a white rot fungus is responsible for lignin decay in a log.

answer.exemplar: Take equal blocks of wood containing lignin and set them up in three treatments: sterile blocks as a control, blocks colonised by the suspected white rot fungus, and blocks from a naturally decayed log for comparison. Keep moisture and temperature the same, then measure the lignin content of each block after a fixed period using a lignin assay, and also record hyphal colonisation under a microscope. A clear fall in lignin in the inoculated blocks with none in the sterile controls shows that the fungus removes lignin.

questions.explanation: Sterile controls and blocks from naturally decayed wood give a baseline and a field comparison, while a lignin assay measures the change directly. Hyphal colonisation confirms the fungus is present.
questions.hint: Use sterile controls and measure lignin before and after.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a basidium forms and releases its spores.
questions.stem: The survey notes ask for a written account of how a basidium forms and releases its spores.

answer.exemplar: A basidium is a club-shaped cell at the surface of a hymenium. Within it the two haploid nuclei of the dikaryon fuse, giving a diploid nucleus, and meiosis then produces four haploid nuclei. Each nucleus migrates out into a small stalk, the sterigma, which is tipped by a single basidiospore. As the spores mature they are held by a droplet and then released, often in a puff when the cap is disturbed, so they are carried away on air currents to colonise new sites.

questions.explanation: The account must link karyogamy and meiosis inside the basidium with the outward movement of the nuclei into externally borne spores. A version leaving the spores inside describes something else.
questions.hint: Trace the nuclei from fusion to the spore.

questions.topic: The sexual cycle as an ordering
questions.learningObjective: Plan a test of the order of events in a fungal sexual cycle.
questions.stem: The projection plan for life cycles asks how a team could confirm the order of events in a fungal sexual cycle.

answer.exemplar: Sample a mating culture at regular intervals, starting when the two haploid strains first touch, and examine each sample under a microscope after staining for nuclei. Record the first appearance of fused hyphae with two separate nuclei, then the first compartment containing a single fused diploid nucleus, and finally the appearance of spores. Plot the timing of these observations, and repeat on separate cultures so the sequence can be checked against several independent matings.

questions.explanation: Stained samples taken through a time course reveal the sequence directly: dikaryotic compartments first, then a fused diploid nucleus, then spores. Replication confirms the order is consistent.
questions.hint: Sample a mating culture repeatedly and watch the nuclei.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why spores from one ascus can differ in mating type.
questions.stem: The projection notes on ascospore mating ask for an explanation of why spores from one ascus can differ in mating type.

answer.exemplar: All the spores in one ascus come from the products of a single meiosis, in which the paired chromosomes separate independently and then cross over. That independent assortment and recombination shuffles the mating type genes, so the resulting ascospores are not all genetically identical even though they share one parent. Two spores of different mating types can therefore fuse with one another, which is exactly what the sexual cycle needs.

questions.explanation: The explanation rests on meiosis generating variation, with independent assortment and crossing over mixing the genes that determine mating type. The spores share one parent but are not clones.
questions.hint: Link the variation to what meiosis does to the genes.

questions.learningObjective: Plan the collection and counting of spores shed from a mushroom cap.
questions.stem: The projection plan for spore prints asks how spores shed from a mushroom cap could be collected and counted.

answer.exemplar: Place a mature cap gill-side down on a sheet of clean paper or over a glass slide inside a sealed chamber with a little water in the base to raise humidity, and leave it for several hours in the dark. The spores that fall onto the paper or slide form a visible print, and the spore colour and density can be recorded. Count the spores in a marked area under a microscope or on a hemocytometer, and estimate the total per cap from the area ratio. Include an unmated cap as a control for contamination.

questions.explanation: A spore print captures the shed spores in a countable deposit, and a marked viewing area allows the density to be converted into a per-cap estimate. Humidity keeps the spores from scattering.
questions.hint: Print the spores onto paper, then count them.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the contribution of clamp connections to a dikaryotic mycelium.
questions.stem: The projection notes on clamp function ask for a written account of what a clamp connection contributes to a dikaryotic mycelium.

answer.exemplar: A clamp connection is a short bridge formed where the two cells of a dikaryotic hypha divide, and it links each cell to its partner so that cytoplasm and organelles can pass between them. Because the nuclei stay in separate compartments, the pair of haploid nuclei is maintained in every cell of the mycelium rather than being fused into one diploid nucleus. This arrangement lets the dikaryon grow, feed and eventually form fruit bodies while remaining genetically haploid in each nucleus.

questions.explanation: The contribution is maintaining the two separate haploid nuclei in each cell, which is what makes the mycelium dikaryotic. The bridge and the separate nuclei belong together in the explanation.
questions.hint: Emphasise nuclear pairing and cytoplasmic exchange.

questions.learningObjective: Account for the benefits a tree gains from an ectomycorrhizal fungus.
questions.stem: The projection notes on woodland trees ask for a written account of the benefits a tree gains from an ectomycorrhizal fungus.

answer.exemplar: The fungal mycelium extends many times further than the roots themselves and reaches into soil pores too small for root hairs, so the tree gains access to more water and to phosphate and other minerals that would otherwise be locked up. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why lignin decay controls the release of carbon from dead wood.
questions.stem: The projection notes on carbon release ask for a written explanation of why lignin decay controls carbon release from wood.

answer.exemplar: Lignin glues the cellulose fibres of wood together and gives the tissue its strength, so a lignin-coated fibre resists the cellulases that fungi secrete. Until the lignin is broken down the cellulose stays shielded and little carbon is released as carbon dioxide or dissolved nutrients. White rot fungi that remove lignin expose the cellulose and so unlock the bulk of the wood carbon, which is why their activity governs how quickly a dead trunk returns its carbon to the ecosystem.

questions.explanation: The explanation depends on lignin acting as a barrier around the cellulose, so lignin decay is the rate-limiting step for carbon release. Treating the two polymers as independent misses that.
questions.hint: Link the lignin barrier to the locked cellulose.
